question: The support agent processes about 9,000 refunds a week through process_refund. Telemetry shows that in 12% of refund calls no verified customer ID from get_customer is in the agent's state when process_refund fires — the model inferred the account from the caller's stated name — and some of those refunded the wrong account. Compliance requires that a refund can never be issued before identity is verified. Which change provides that guarantee?
options: A tool-call interception hook that blocks process_refund unless a verified customer ID from get_customer is already in state
A PostToolUse hook on process_refund that detects an unverified refund and issues a compensating reversal once the charge has been applied
Having process_refund's MCP handler return an isError business error with isRetryable false whenever it can't find a verified customer ID
tool_choice forcing get_customer on the first turn of every conversation, then leaving selection on auto for the turns after that
explanation: Only a pre-call gate makes this deterministic: the refund cannot execute until the verification step has completed and recorded an ID, so the 12% never reaches the payment system. The same hook hands the blocked case to the escalation workflow.
wrongAnswerNotes: A compensating reversal fires after the money has already moved on someone else's account, which is remediation rather than a guarantee. Forcing the identity lookup on the opening turn protects the first refund and leaves every later one in a multi-issue conversation unguarded. Returning a business error is the closest alternative and still leaves the reroute to the model's discretion, and it assumes the server can see verification state it may not hold.

question: You are hand-writing the support agent's loop around the Messages API. What should decide whether the loop runs another tool iteration or returns the final answer?
options: Whether stop_reason is tool_use (keep going) or end_turn (stop)
Whether a fixed iteration cap tuned to the task has been reached
Whether the assistant's text still mentions needing to call a tool
Whether the tool results have stopped changing between iterations
explanation: Loop control flow is driven by the protocol's own completion signal: while stop_reason is tool_use the model is waiting on tool results, and end_turn means it has finished reasoning and the reply is ready to present.
wrongAnswerNotes: Reading the assistant's prose for a mention of further tool use makes control flow depend on wording that varies run to run — the documented anti-pattern. A fixed iteration cap belongs in the design as a runaway safety valve, not as the primary stopping rule, since it fires on well-behaved conversations too. Watching for tool results to stop changing infers completion from the data instead of reading the signal the protocol already gives you.

question: A customer asks about a delayed shipment. The agent calls lookup_order, your harness executes it against the order service, and it returns the order record successfully. What has to happen for the model to reason about that record on its next turn?
options: Nothing — the API executes the tool and folds the result in for you
Attach the record to the tool's definition, which is re-read each turn
The MCP server streams the record into the model's context on completion
Append a tool result block keyed to the call id and resend the history
explanation: Tool execution is the harness's responsibility. The conversation history is the only channel into the model, so the result has to be appended as a tool result block referencing the originating call id and sent back with the next request.
wrongAnswerNotes: Neither the MCP server nor the API pushes anything into an in-flight context — the model sees exactly what your next request contains, and an out-of-band delivery would leave the history inconsistent with what it read. Tool definitions are static declarations read at selection time; they carry no runtime data.

question: The agent has spent six tool calls establishing that a customer was double-charged across two order numbers, and the dispute now needs a human. The escalation queue receives a ticket only — the agents working it have no access to the conversation transcript. What should escalate_to_human carry?
options: The full turn-by-turn transcript plus every raw tool result gathered
Customer ID, root cause so far, amounts and orders, and next action
The customer ID and issue category, so the human forms a fresh view
A sentiment read and an urgency score so the queue can be prioritised
explanation: A structured handoff exists precisely because the receiving human lacks the transcript. Identity, the analysis reached so far, the figures involved, and a recommendation let them continue the case rather than restart it.
wrongAnswerNotes: Forwarding the whole transcript transfers unprocessed material and leaves the human to redo the reasoning the agent already did. Sending only identity and category discards a completed investigation and makes the customer repeat themselves. Sentiment and urgency help route the case but say nothing about its state.

question: Policy caps autonomous refunds at $500, and anything larger must go to a human. In load testing the model still proposes refunds above the cap in a small fraction of edge cases, and the business needs the cap to hold on every one of them. Which mechanism enforces it?
options: MCP-side validation rejecting over-cap amounts with an isError business error
An interception hook that blocks the over-cap call and reroutes it to escalation
tool_choice set to any on refund turns so the model must call an approved tool
A PostToolUse hook that raises an alert once an over-cap refund has been paid out
explanation: Interception happens before the call leaves the harness, so an over-cap refund never executes, and the same hook performs the reroute in one step — both halves of the policy, guaranteed.
wrongAnswerNotes: An alert after payout observes a breach that has already happened. Server-side rejection does stop the charge and is the closest alternative, but it leaves the escalation to whatever the model decides to do with the error it gets back. Forcing a tool call constrains which tool runs, never the value carried in its arguments.

question: get_customer and lookup_order each carry a one-line description, and the agent keeps sending order questions to the identity tool. Which change to the descriptions fixes the misrouting most directly?
options: List the two tools in the order the support workflow normally uses them
Move the choice between the two into the system prompt as a routing rule
Name the backend service each tool queries and the team that owns it
Say when each applies — order number present versus verifying identity
explanation: Descriptions are what the model reads at selection time, so the fix belongs there: explicit boundary language naming the condition that separates the two tools removes the ambiguity causing the misroute.
wrongAnswerNotes: Ordering the list relies on a positional effect that is not a dependable selection mechanism. Naming the backend and its owner is useful documentation for engineers and says nothing about when to pick one tool over the other. Moving the rule to the system prompt shifts the signal away from the point where the decision is actually made.

question: Every failure inside process_refund currently returns the string "Operation failed." The agent now retries policy-blocked refunds and gives up on brief outages. What should the tool return instead?
options: A success result with an empty refund object when the refund is refused
The payment provider's raw rejection payload with its internal rule ids
An error category, a retryable flag, and a short human-readable reason
The same string, with the harness retrying twice before surfacing it
explanation: Recovery decisions need machine-readable signal. A category, an explicit retryable flag, and a plain-language reason let the agent retry an outage, stop retrying a policy refusal, and explain that refusal to the customer.
wrongAnswerNotes: The raw provider payload is rich but unusable — internal rule identifiers are not something the agent can act on or repeat to a customer. Dressing a refusal as an empty success turns a failure into misinformation. Retrying inside the harness hides business refusals the agent is supposed to explain, and retries them pointlessly.

question: The support agent has accumulated 18 tools as new backend systems were connected, and it now picks the wrong one often enough that first-contact resolution has slipped. Sharpening the descriptions has helped only marginally. What is the most effective architectural change?
options: Group the 18 tools into namespaces the agent filters before choosing
Order the tool list so the most frequently used tools appear first
Split the work across role-scoped agents with only their own tools
Add a meta-tool the agent calls to ask which tool it should use
explanation: Selection reliability degrades as the option count grows, so the fix is to shrink each decision. Role-scoped agents each hold a handful of relevant tools, which is a configuration control rather than a hint.
wrongAnswerNotes: Namespaces and list ordering both reorganise the same 18 options without reducing how many the agent must weigh at the moment of choice. A meta-tool answers a selection problem with another selection problem, and the router itself has to be chosen correctly first.

question: In long multi-issue sessions the agent starts quoting a disputed charge as "about $43" when the record says $43.27, because earlier turns have been summarised. What preserves the figures?
options: Keep amounts, dates and order ids verbatim in a block outside the summary
Raise max_tokens so replies have room to restate the full case detail
Summarise on every turn so the running summary never drifts far
Instruct the summariser to preserve every figure at its full precision
explanation: Summarisation is lossy by design, so precise transactional facts should not live inside it. A persistent case-facts block carried verbatim in every request keeps the exact figures available however far the conversation runs.
wrongAnswerNotes: Instructing the summariser to keep full precision is a request against a process whose whole purpose is compression, and it degrades quietly. Summarising more often applies that same lossy step more times, intensifying the failure rather than fixing it. max_tokens governs how much the model may write, not what it can still see.

question: Your support agent resolves about 70% of contacts without a human, and its escalation rule is currently a single line in the system prompt. You are rewriting it as explicit criteria with worked examples. Select TWO conditions that should trigger an immediate handoff to a human.
options: The conversation has run past the agent's usual number of tool calls
The request falls outside what the written policy addresses either way
The customer explicitly asks to speak to a human rather than the agent
The customer's message registers as frustrated on a sentiment classifier
The agent's self-reported confidence in its answer falls below 0.7
explanation: Two triggers are first-class: a stated preference for a human, honoured immediately without a demonstration attempt, and a policy gap or exception the agent has no authority to decide. Both are unambiguous facts about the case rather than proxies for it.
wrongAnswerNotes: Sentiment measures mood, and an annoyed customer with a simple return is still a case the agent should resolve. Turn count tracks how long the work took, not whether it exceeded the agent's authority. Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated — the agent tends to be most confident exactly where it is wrong.

question: Yesterday you ran a long memory-leak investigation in a Claude Code session you named leak-hunt, and you have run several other sessions in that directory since. How do you pick that investigation back up?
options: A new session in the same repo, relying on CLAUDE.md for the context
claude -p "carry on with the leak investigation from yesterday"
claude --continue, which reopens the last session in this directory
claude --resume leak-hunt, restoring that named session's context
explanation: Named resumption is the mechanism for returning to one specific prior conversation: the session is addressed by name, so the accumulated investigation comes back intact regardless of what has run since.
wrongAnswerNotes: Continuing the most recent session reopens whichever conversation ran last, which the stem rules out. A fresh non-interactive prompt starts with no memory of yesterday at all. CLAUDE.md restores project conventions, not the findings a particular investigation accumulated.

question: You want to continue last week's refactoring session, but the team has since merged large changes across most of the files it read, so its tool results describe code that no longer exists. What is the reliable move?
options: Start fresh, seeding the new session with a summary of the prior conclusions
Resume it and ask for a re-read of each file that changed since then
Resume it and run /compact first so the stale results are compressed
Resume it as it stands, since file changes are detected automatically
explanation: Resumption is worth it when the prior context is mostly still true. Once the evidence has gone stale, the conclusions are the part worth keeping and the outdated tool results are the part to leave behind.
wrongAnswerNotes: Compacting the stale results yields a shorter version of the same wrong picture. Re-reading the changed files is workable for light drift and here leaves old and new descriptions of the same code side by side for the model to blend. Nothing re-verifies files automatically; stale results simply sit in context as if current.

question: A new teammate's sessions ignore the team's coding standards, which the lead keeps in their own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. Select TWO statements that correctly describe the fix and how to confirm it.
options: Each subdirectory needs its own copy for the rules to apply within it
/memory shows which memory files the current session actually loaded
The standards belong in the project's CLAUDE.md, committed to the repo
Copying the lead's file into each teammate's home directory shares them
Standards belong in .claude/settings.json, which the repo already ships
explanation: User-level configuration never travels through version control, so team standards belong at project level where a clone carries them. The /memory command is the diagnostic that shows exactly which files a session picked up.
wrongAnswerNotes: Hand-copying works once and then drifts with the next edit, since nothing keeps the copies in step. settings.json carries permissions and tool configuration rather than standards prose. Per-directory copies duplicate maintenance for rules that already apply repository-wide from the project file.

question: The project's CLAUDE.md has reached 2,000 lines spanning testing, API conventions, deployment and styling, and every session loads all of it. What is the recommended reorganisation?
options: Cut it to a 200-line summary and let the model infer the specifics
Move the whole file into each developer's user-level configuration
Split it into topic files in .claude/rules/, scoped by path
Turn each section into a slash command developers run when relevant
explanation: Focused rule files are the modular alternative to one growing document, and path scoping means a file loads only when the work touches matching paths — less irrelevant context, and a far easier file to maintain.
wrongAnswerNotes: Trimming to a summary discards the specifics that made the conventions enforceable in the first place. Moving everything user-level unshares the team's configuration and guarantees divergence. Converting always-relevant standards into commands makes them opt-in and easy to forget.

question: Your /analyze-architecture skill floods the main conversation with thousands of lines of exploration, crowding out the task you actually asked about. Which SKILL.md frontmatter option addresses this?
options: allowed-tools, restricting the skill to read-only operations
context: fork, which runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context
argument-hint, narrowing each invocation to a smaller target
model, moving the skill onto a cheaper and smaller model tier
explanation: Forking gives the skill its own context to work in, so the exploration happens out of the way and only the distilled result comes back to the main conversation.
wrongAnswerNotes: Restricting tools changes what the skill may do, and read-only exploration is precisely what is producing the flood. An argument hint narrows what the skill examines rather than where its output accumulates. A smaller model changes cost and quality, not which context the output lands in.

question: You are writing a /scaffold-component skill that must be able to create files but must never be able to run shell commands, whatever its instructions end up saying. How do you enforce that?
options: Set allowed-tools in the frontmatter to file tools, omitting Bash
State prominently in the SKILL.md body that Bash must never be used
Add a hook that scans the rendered instructions for shell commands
Run the skill only in plan mode, where commands are proposed not run
explanation: Tool restrictions declared in frontmatter bound what the skill can invoke while it runs. That is a configuration guarantee rather than an instruction the model may or may not follow.
wrongAnswerNotes: A prominent instruction is still an instruction, with a failure rate a guarantee cannot tolerate. Plan mode changes the whole session's workflow rather than restricting this one skill, and it depends on every caller remembering. Scanning the instructions inspects text, when the risk is what the skill actually invokes at runtime.

question: Two jobs land in the same morning: a one-line null check in a function with a clear stack trace, and swapping the codebase's HTTP client across 45 files with several viable approaches. How should plan mode be applied?
options: Plan mode for the null check; direct execution for the client swap
Direct execution for the one-line null check; plan mode for the client swap
Plan mode for both, since a reviewed plan lowers risk on any change
Direct execution for both, since planning changes nothing that ships
explanation: Plan mode earns its overhead where scale and competing approaches make the design decision the risky part. A single-file fix with a stack trace pointing at the line has no such decision to make.
wrongAnswerNotes: Planning both taxes a trivial fix with ceremony that produces nothing. Executing both directly commits to one approach across 45 files before anyone has compared the alternatives, which is where the expensive rework comes from. The inverted pairing applies each mode to the task that least benefits from it.

question: A multi-phase feature starts with a broad discovery sweep across an unfamiliar service before any code is written, and that sweep alone keeps exhausting the window. Which approach does the guide recommend?
options: Skip discovery and let the implementation phase read files as it goes
Split discovery across several sessions and merge the notes by hand
Run discovery in the main session and /compact once it has finished
Run discovery through the Explore subagent, which returns a summary
explanation: Delegating the verbose phase keeps the bulk of the discovery out of the main conversation entirely — the subagent absorbs the reading and hands back the summary the implementation phase actually needs.
wrongAnswerNotes: Compacting afterwards is a genuine relief valve, and by then the window has already been exhausted, with compaction lossy about material it has not finished using. Splitting across sessions puts the merge burden on you and loses the connections between phases. Reading lazily during implementation rediscovers the same ground with less structure.

question: Several hours into exploring a legacy codebase, the agent starts answering from "typical patterns" instead of the classes it identified earlier. Select TWO practices that counteract this.
options: Re-paste the full list of discovered classes into the chat periodically
Record key findings in a scratchpad file the agent consults afterwards
Send verbose investigation to subagents that return only summaries
Move to a model with a larger window and keep accumulating as before
Instruct the agent to answer from discovered code, not general knowledge
explanation: Both practices manage what occupies the window. A scratchpad keeps precise findings on disk, outside the degrading conversation, and delegation keeps the high-volume reading out of the main session so its context stays coordination-sized.
wrongAnswerNotes: Re-pasting the class list adds bulk to a context that is already saturated, which is the condition being treated. A larger window buys time at higher cost and reaches the same degradation later. Instructing the agent to prefer discovered code assumes that code is still legible in context — an instruction cannot restore a signal already crowded out.

question: Midway through an extended exploration session, verbose discovery output is filling the window and answers are visibly degrading, but the findings so far are sound and you are not ready to stop. What helps immediately?
options: /memory, reloading the memory files to refresh the session's context
/rewind, rolling back to a checkpoint before the exploration began
/compact, condensing the accumulated conversation so the session continues
/rules, reloading the rule files so conventions are back in context
explanation: Compaction is the in-session relief valve for exactly this: the accumulated discovery output is condensed into a summary, freeing room while the session and its conclusions carry on.
wrongAnswerNotes: Rewinding to a checkpoint discards the findings made since that point along with the noise, and the stem says those findings are sound. Reloading memory files or rule files adds configuration back into context; neither touches the conversation bulk causing the degradation.

question: To save a round trip, two research subagents have begun calling each other directly to exchange intermediate data rather than returning through the coordinator. Runs now fail intermittently, and the traces no longer show which stage produced a bad finding. What is the sound architecture?
options: Give each subagent the others' definitions so they can self-coordinate
Keep the direct links but log every exchange to a shared audit file
Route inter-subagent traffic and error handling via the coordinator
Give both subagents a shared memory area to read and write between calls
explanation: Hub-and-spoke keeps one component responsible for routing, error handling and information flow. Every exchange passes a point that can observe it, which is what makes a failure attributable to a stage.
wrongAnswerNotes: Logging the direct exchanges records the tangle without untangling it, and the coordinator still cannot intervene. Sharing definitions or a memory area makes the coupling worse: both give subagents more ways to reach each other outside the path the system is meant to observe.

question: The coordinator invokes all four subagents on every request. Traces show that on one-line factual questions — "when was the standard ratified?" — the document-analysis, synthesis and report subagents each run and contribute nothing the search agent had not already returned. What should change?
options: Keep the pipeline but shorten each subagent's system prompt to save cost
Cache simple queries so the pipeline runs once per repeated question
Run all four in parallel so the unnecessary ones add no wall-clock time
Have it assess each query and invoke only the subagents needed
explanation: Deciding which subagents a query actually needs is part of the coordinator's job. Analysing the request and dispatching selectively is what separates an orchestrator from a fixed pipeline with a model in front of it.
wrongAnswerNotes: Shortening prompts trims the cost of work that should not be happening at all. Parallelising hides the latency and still pays for every subagent, and tokens are the larger part of the bill. Caching helps only on repeats, so the first instance of every simple question still runs the full pipeline.

question: Finished reports read well but come back thin on some subtopics of broad questions, even though every subagent completed its assignment successfully. Which coordinator pattern addresses this?
options: Evaluate the synthesis for coverage gaps, re-delegate, then re-synthesise
Have the report generator fill thin sections from general knowledge
Run every subagent twice and merge the two passes into one report
Add a reviewer subagent that scores the report and lists its weaknesses
explanation: Coverage gaps come from the decomposition, so the repair has to loop back into it: inspect the synthesis, dispatch targeted follow-up research where the gaps are, and synthesise again until coverage holds.
wrongAnswerNotes: A reviewer that scores and lists weaknesses is genuinely useful and still ships the thin report — detection without a repair path changes nothing. Running everything twice doubles the cost with no gap detection aiming the second pass. Filling thin sections from general knowledge produces uncited assertions in a report whose value is its citations.

question: Your coordinator's prompt describes delegation clearly, its subagent definitions look right, and at runtime it does all the research itself without ever spawning anything. What is the most likely cause?
options: Its allowedTools omits Task, so it cannot spawn any subagent
Its model tier lacks the reasoning depth that delegation calls for
The prompt describes delegation without naming particular subagents
The subagent descriptions are too vague for the coordinator to match
explanation: Spawning goes through the Task tool, and a coordinator that has not been granted it has no mechanism to delegate no matter how the prompt reads. Capability configuration beats instruction here.
wrongAnswerNotes: Vague descriptions and an under-specified prompt both degrade matching, and they would produce poor delegation rather than none at all. Model tier affects how well a coordinator decomposes work, not whether the delegation call is available to it.

question: In the research system the synthesis subagent returns coherent but generic conclusions that do not reflect what the search and document-analysis subagents found, even though the coordinator ran cleanly and both upstream subagents returned good results. You built the coordinator assuming each subagent it spawns can see the coordinator's conversation so far. What is the fix?
options: Raise the synthesis subagent's max_tokens ceiling so it can take in the upstream history
Enable a shared memory store so synthesis can read the coordinator's transcript on demand
Subagents run isolated, so pass the upstream findings and source metadata in the prompt
The coordinator's allowedTools omits Task, so the synthesis agent spawned without inputs
explanation: Subagent context isolation is the rule: a spawned agent sees only what its prompt contains. Synthesis was asked to combine findings it was never given, so the coordinator has to pass them, with their source metadata, explicitly.
wrongAnswerNotes: A missing Task permission would mean the subagent never spawned at all, and the stem says it ran. A shared memory store abandons the isolation model rather than working within it, and couples agents that should stay independent. More output room cannot help a model reason over history that was never in its context — the deficit is input, not length.

question: The synthesis agent needs a quick date or name check in roughly 85% of its runs, and routing each one through the coordinator is adding real latency. The remaining checks need genuine investigation. What fits?
options: Have the search agent pre-cache context around each source in advance
Have it batch every check and send them all once synthesis is done
Give it the full search toolset so it never needs a round trip at all
Give it a narrow verify_fact tool and route harder checks upward
explanation: Scoped cross-role access is the designed middle ground: one narrow tool covers the high-frequency simple case, while anything requiring judgement still goes through the coordinator that owns the routing.
wrongAnswerNotes: Handing over the full search toolset over-provisions the agent and reintroduces the cross-specialisation misuse that scoping exists to prevent. Batching checks to the end creates a blocking dependency and delays discovering that a claim does not hold. Speculative caching cannot know what synthesis will want to verify.

question: Subagents spend a large share of their tool calls just discovering what exists — listing document collections, probing for issue summaries, checking which schemas are present. Which MCP capability reduces that?
options: Expose those catalogues as MCP resources the agents can browse in advance
Hard-code the current inventory into every subagent's system prompt
Add a describe_available_data tool each agent calls once at startup
Raise each subagent's tool-call budget so the exploration is affordable
explanation: Resources are the protocol's primitive for exposing content catalogues. Agents see what is available without spending calls to find out, so discovery becomes a lookup rather than an expedition.
wrongAnswerNotes: A bespoke inventory tool rebuilds the same capability as another tool call, which is the cost being removed — the closest wrong answer here. Hard-coding the inventory goes stale the moment the data changes. Raising the budget pays for the inefficiency instead of removing it.

question: Your research coordinator aggregates findings from six subagents into one long input, then runs a final pass to produce the report. The report reliably reflects the first and last subagents' findings but frequently omits material from the middle three, even though all six returned good content. What most directly mitigates this?
options: Merge the six sections into one continuous narrative with no headers between them
Order the six sections by whichever subagent happened to finish its work first
Raise the final pass's max_tokens ceiling so there is room for every section in full
Lead with a key-findings summary, then set detailed sections under clear headers
explanation: This is the lost-in-the-middle effect: long inputs are processed most reliably at their start and end. Putting the key findings first and giving each detailed section an explicit header changes both where material sits and how findable it is.
wrongAnswerNotes: More output room governs how much the model may write, not which parts of a long input it attends to. Ordering by completion time is arbitrary and buries a different three sections instead. Removing the headers makes middle content harder to locate rather than easier.

question: You are specifying how the web-search subagent reports back when a source times out, and separately when a well-formed query simply matches nothing. The coordinator has to decide whether to retry, re-delegate, or record a genuine coverage gap. Select TWO behaviours that are correct.
options: Report access failures separately from valid empty result sets
Return an empty result marked successful whenever a search fails
Halt the whole workflow and surface any failure to the operator
Recover locally from transient faults; escalate the rest with partials
Collapse all failures to one status so coordinator handling stays simple
explanation: Propagation should be layered and honest: fix locally what is locally fixable, hand up the rest with partial results and a note of what was attempted, and never let "the search broke" and "the search found nothing" arrive as the same signal.
wrongAnswerNotes: Marking a failure as an empty success is silent suppression, and the coordinator then treats a gap as a finding. Halting on any single failure makes one flaky source fatal when partial coverage was available. A single flattened status is simple for the coordinator and strips exactly the context its recovery decision needs.

question: Final reports assert findings but cite nothing. Each summarisation step compresses attribution away, so by synthesis time nobody can say which claim came from where. What is the structural fix?
options: Have each summariser append a bibliography of everything it consulted
Reduce the pipeline to a single summarisation step before synthesis
Have subagents emit claim-source mappings every stage must preserve
Have the report generator attach citations once the draft is complete
explanation: Attribution survives only if it travels as data. A structured mapping from each claim to its source is carried through every hop, so synthesis merges attributed claims instead of anonymous ones.
wrongAnswerNotes: A bibliography records what was read without binding any source to any claim, so the mapping still cannot be recovered. Attaching citations after the draft means inventing them, which is worse than none in a research product. Cutting to one summarisation step reduces how many times attribution is stripped, and the remaining step still strips it.

question: You have finished a thorough analysis of a module and now want to develop two competing refactoring strategies from that same baseline, without either exploration contaminating the other. Which capability fits?
options: fork_session, branching two independent lines from the shared analysis
One session, asking the model to set the first strategy aside midway
/compact between the two strategies to clear the first from context
Two fresh sessions, each seeded by pasting the analysis conclusions
explanation: Forking exists for divergent exploration: both branches start from the completed analysis and evolve separately, so the comparison is clean and the analysis is not paid for twice.
wrongAnswerNotes: Seeding two fresh sessions by hand approximates the baseline with a lossy summary and sets it up twice over. Compaction reduces one session's context; it does not branch it. Asking the model to set earlier reasoning aside is not something context supports — nothing is selectively forgotten on request.

question: The MCP servers behind your productivity agent return timestamps three different ways — Unix epoch, ISO 8601, and a numeric status code — and the agent keeps misreading them. What normalises them reliably?
options: A note in each tool's description explaining that tool's own format
A system prompt section listing each format and how to interpret it
Few-shot examples showing the model parsing all three formats
A PostToolUse hook rewriting results to one format before use
explanation: A result-interception hook transforms tool output deterministically before the model ever reads it, so the parsing stops being a judgement the model has to make correctly on every single call.
wrongAnswerNotes: Prompt sections, per-tool notes and worked examples all teach the model to interpret the formats, which works most of the time and fails at some rate forever. Normalising in code makes the variation invisible to the model instead of asking it to cope with it.

question: One workflow reviews pull requests against the same five aspects every run. Another investigates production incidents, where each finding determines what to look at next. Which decomposition suits which?
options: Prompt chaining for both, since fixed steps are easier to regress-test
Adaptive decomposition for the review; prompt chaining for incidents
Adaptive decomposition for both, since flexibility costs little here
Prompt chaining for the review; adaptive decomposition for incidents
explanation: The choice follows how much of the path is knowable in advance. A five-aspect review is fully specified before it starts, while an incident's next step only exists once the previous one has reported.
wrongAnswerNotes: Making both adaptive pays runtime planning overhead on a workflow with no uncertainty to plan around. Making both fixed forces an investigation down steps written before any evidence existed. The inverted pairing gives each workflow the structure that fits it worst.

question: A team lead asks the agent to "add comprehensive tests to this legacy service." The service is 60,000 lines across four packages with no existing suite, and nobody on the current team knows where the risk concentrates or which modules depend on which. How should the work be decomposed?
options: Generate the whole suite in one pass with the codebase in full view
Start with the files carrying the most recent commits and work back
Map the structure, rank by impact, then plan and adapt as it unfolds
Write tests file by file in directory order until coverage is complete
explanation: Open-ended work calls for adaptive decomposition: understand the terrain first, prioritise where the risk concentrates, and let the plan change as each step reveals dependencies nobody knew about.
wrongAnswerNotes: Directory order spends effort in a sequence that has nothing to do with risk. One comprehensive pass asks a single request to do the discovery and the work at once. Recency is a proxy for activity, and legacy risk tends to sit in the old code nobody has touched.

question: The team shares a GitHub MCP server that needs an auth token, and you also run a personal experimental server nobody else should inherit. Select TWO steps that configure this correctly.
options: Put the shared server in a committed .mcp.json so clones receive it
Put the shared server in ~/.claude.json to keep the token out of git
Supply its token by variable expansion rather than an inline value
Disable built-in tools that overlap so selection cannot collide
Register each of the server's tools in project settings to expose them
explanation: Project scope distributes team tooling through version control, and environment variable expansion keeps the credential itself out of the repository. The personal server stays in user scope, where it affects only you.
wrongAnswerNotes: Putting the shared server in user configuration does keep the token out of git and defeats the point, since teammates never receive it — the sharpest trap here. Tools from a connected server are discovered at connection time, so there is nothing to register by hand. Disabling overlapping built-ins is not required and removes capability the agent may still need.

question: The agent must (a) find every file following the project's test naming convention and (b) find every place the identifier PaymentDeclinedError appears in code. Select TWO correct tool choices.
options: Grep for PaymentDeclinedError across file contents
Glob for PaymentDeclinedError across file contents
Grep with a filename pattern to collect the test files
Bash with grep -r for both, since a shell covers paths and text
Glob with a pattern such as **/*.test.tsx for the test files
explanation: The division is clean: path patterns are matched by Glob, file contents are searched by Grep. Each half of this task maps onto exactly one of them.
wrongAnswerNotes: The two swapped options put each tool in the other's territory. Shelling out works mechanically, gives up the structured output the agent consumes, and expresses the path-pattern match considerably less clearly than the tool built for it.

question: An Edit on a legacy file fails because the anchor text the agent chose occurs in six places, so the unique-match requirement cannot be met — and only one of the six should change. What is the standard fallback?
options: Re-run the Edit with a replace-all option so all six are updated
Switch to Bash and apply the change with a sed expression
Remove five occurrences first so the remaining match is unique
Read the file in full, then Write the complete modified contents back
explanation: When a file's repetition defeats unique matching, loading it and writing it back performs the change reliably — the documented fallback for exactly this failure.
wrongAnswerNotes: Replace-all changes all six sites when the stem says one should change. Stream editing swaps a controlled file operation for a fragile expression with no verification. Deleting occurrences to satisfy the tool mutilates the code to fit the mechanism.

question: You use a /scratch-notes command constantly, but it reflects only your own workflow and should not appear for teammates when they clone the repository. Where does the command file belong?
options: In ~/.claude/commands/ in your home directory
In .claude/commands/ with a prefix marking it personal
In .claude/rules/ with a glob matching your username
In the root CLAUDE.md under a commands heading
explanation: Command scope mirrors intent. User-scoped commands live in the home directory and stay visible to you alone, while the project directory is shared with everyone through version control.
wrongAnswerNotes: A naming prefix inside the repository still ships the command to every clone; a convention is not a scoping mechanism. CLAUDE.md carries project context rather than command definitions. Path-scoped rules condition on which files are being edited, not on who is running the session.

question: Test files sit beside the code they cover throughout the repository, and one set of testing conventions should apply to them wherever they are. What is the most maintainable mechanism?
options: A file in .claude/rules/ whose paths glob matches the test file pattern
A skill per code area carrying that area's own testing conventions
A CLAUDE.md in every directory that happens to contain test files
A testing section in the root CLAUDE.md the model applies by inference
explanation: Glob-based path scoping applies conventions by file type regardless of where the file lives, and the rule loads only when matching files are in play — which is the case the mechanism was designed for.
wrongAnswerNotes: Per-directory files multiply maintenance and miss any directory somebody forgets. A root section is always loaded and leaves application to inference. Skills need invoking, so conventions that should apply automatically become opt-in.

question: A CSV-to-JSON transformation keeps coming back subtly wrong from a prose description: nulls become empty strings, dates lose their timezone, and the two interact so that a null timestamp lands as "1970-01-01". What is the most effective way to iterate?
options: Give two or three worked input/output pairs, raising all three at once
Move to a larger model and resend the same description unchanged
Fix the three defects one at a time across separate follow-up runs
Restate the description in much greater detail and rerun the whole task
explanation: Concrete input/output pairs communicate a transformation far more precisely than prose, and interacting defects belong in one message so the fixes can be designed against each other.
wrongAnswerNotes: More prose restates an ambiguity in more words. Fixing interacting defects sequentially invites each fix to reopen the last, which is the specific case the guide separates from independent issues. A larger model inherits the same unclear specification.

question: Your CI job must run Claude Code on a runner with no terminal attached, and the pipeline then posts each finding as an inline comment on the pull request, keyed to a file and a line number. Parsing the prose output has already broken twice this month. Which invocation matches the requirement?
options: claude piped through grep to pull findings from the prose
claude --headless, with a --format json flag for parsing
claude -p alone, with the pipeline regex-parsing the prose
claude -p, with --output-format json and --json-schema set
explanation: Non-interactive execution comes from the print flag, machine-readable output from the JSON output format, and a stable shape the pipeline can rely on from the schema flag. Together they remove both the hang and the parsing.
wrongAnswerNotes: Printing without a schema solves the hang and still leaves the pipeline matching patterns against free text whose wording changes run to run. The headless and format flags in the other invocation are not flags the CLI offers. Piping an interactive invocation through grep still waits for a terminal that CI does not have.

question: Reviews re-run on every new commit to a pull request. On a branch with nine commits the bot posted the same four findings nine times over, and the team has now muted it entirely. How should re-reviews be designed?
options: Hash each finding's file and line and drop repeats in the pipeline
Limit the bot to one review per pull request whatever follows it
Include the prior findings; ask for new or unaddressed ones
Review only the newest commit's diff, in isolation from the rest
explanation: Suppressing duplicates is a context design problem. Giving the reviewer its own previous output and asking explicitly for the delta keeps coverage complete while the repetition stops.
wrongAnswerNotes: Reviewing the newest diff alone misses problems that appear only in how it interacts with earlier commits. Hashing file and line breaks the moment a diff shifts line numbers, and it cannot distinguish a fixed finding from one detected again. Capping at one review leaves everything pushed afterwards unreviewed.

question: A GitHub Actions job runs Claude Code to review each pull request. It must run one prompt and exit without ever waiting for interactive input, it must be prevented from looping or spiralling in cost on a pathological diff, and it must not carry over state from any previous run. Select TWO flags that directly serve these requirements.
options: --lazy, to defer tool calls until needed and hold the cost down
--dangerously-skip-permissions, so the job never stalls on a prompt
--max-turns, to cap how many agentic turns a single run may take
--continue, to resume the most recent session so prior context carries
-p (or --print), to run the prompt non-interactively and then exit
explanation: Non-interactive execution comes from the print flag, and a turn cap is the safety net that stops a runaway from spiralling in cost on a pathological diff. Together they cover the requirements as stated.
wrongAnswerNotes: Resuming the most recent session is a real flag doing the opposite of what is asked, since the job must not carry state forward. Skipping permission prompts is real and common in CI, and it addresses neither non-interactivity nor bounding. The deferred-tool-call flag does not exist. Note that a turn cap is a CI safety net, distinct from ordinary loop termination, which is driven by stop_reason.

question: Your review prompt says "be conservative and only report high-confidence findings," and false positives are still high. What does effective precision engineering look like instead?
options: Report everything but sort the findings by stated confidence
Name the issue types to report, those to skip, and the boundary
Strengthen the wording to be very conservative for more emphasis
Review fewer files per run so each gets more careful attention
explanation: Vague conservatism has no operational content, so it does not transfer. Categorical criteria — what counts as reportable, what does not, and where the line sits — give the model a decision rule it can actually apply.
wrongAnswerNotes: Intensifying the wording amplifies an instruction that was never operable. Sorting by self-stated confidence reorders the noise instead of reducing it, and that confidence is poorly calibrated in the first place. Reviewing fewer files applies the same faulty judgement to a smaller sample.

question: Findings in the style category run at roughly 70% false positives, and developers have started dismissing the security findings too. What is the right operational move while the prompts are fixed?
options: Downgrade every style finding to informational and keep posting them
Post more style findings to demonstrate why the category matters
Add a banner asking developers to bear with the tuning in progress
Turn the style category off entirely until its precision has improved
explanation: A high false-positive category is contagious: it teaches developers to dismiss the whole reviewer. Taking it out of circulation protects the credibility of the categories that are accurate while its prompts are repaired offline.
wrongAnswerNotes: Downgrading severity and adding a banner both keep the noise flowing and ask developers to absorb a cost the configuration could simply remove. Increasing the volume doubles down on the very output destroying trust.

question: The reviewer keeps flagging your codebase's accepted idioms — deliberate switch fall-throughs marked by comments — as bugs, and detailed prose instructions have not stopped it. What is the most effective addition?
options: Paired examples of accepted idioms and real bugs, with the reasons
An instruction to defer to the codebase's own established conventions
A rule treating any construct carrying an explanatory comment as fine
An exclusion list of the files where these idioms currently appear
explanation: Where prose has failed to convey a judgement boundary, examples carry it. Contrasted cases with the reasoning attached teach a distinction the model can extend to idioms nobody enumerated.
wrongAnswerNotes: Telling the model to defer to conventions names the goal without transferring the judgement — it still cannot tell a convention from a defect. Treating any commented construct as acceptable is defeated by the first commented bug. Excluding files exempts exactly the code most worth reviewing.

question: Developers dismiss a steady share of findings, and you want to learn systematically which code constructs produce them rather than reading dismissals one at a time. What should the finding schema carry?
options: A timestamp and reviewer id for every dismissal that is recorded
A free-text note from the model explaining why it flagged this
A confidence score the model assigns to each finding it reports
A detected_pattern field naming the construct that triggered it
explanation: Recording which construct triggered each finding turns dismissals into an analysable dataset: patterns with high dismissal rates become visible, and the prompts responsible can be targeted precisely.
wrongAnswerNotes: A free-text rationale is readable one finding at a time and does not aggregate. A self-assigned confidence score is uncalibrated and, more to the point, does not identify the construct at fault. Timestamps and reviewer ids describe who dismissed what and when, not what the reviewer was reacting to.

question: Your pipeline runs three Claude-backed jobs: a pre-merge review developers wait on, nightly test generation, and a weekly architecture audit. Finance has asked the team to take the Message Batches API's 50% saving wherever it is safe to do so. Select TWO accurate statements.
options: Multi-turn tool calling is supported within a single batch request
Results return in submission order, so responses match positionally
Batches complete within an hour in off-peak windows, so gating works
Overnight test generation and weekly audits suit batch processing
Blocking pre-merge checks should stay on the synchronous API
explanation: The rule runs in both directions: latency-tolerant, non-blocking jobs are the profile the discount is built for, and anything a developer is waiting on cannot sit inside a window with no latency guarantee.
wrongAnswerNotes: There is no completion-time guarantee at any hour, so nothing about a merge gate can be built on one. Tools cannot be executed mid-request inside a batch. Responses are correlated by the custom identifier attached to each request, not by their position in the results.

question: When the same Claude Code session that produced a change also reviews it, the review is noticeably gentle and misses issues an independent run catches. What explains this and what follows from it?
options: It is being agreeable; instruct it to review far more harshly
Sampling variance is the cause; review at temperature zero
Reviews need a larger model tier than the one that generated
It retains the reasoning that made the code; review separately
explanation: A session carries the rationale that produced the change, which makes it far less likely to question decisions it already made. A fresh instance evaluates the code on its own terms.
wrongAnswerNotes: Reading this as agreeableness misdiagnoses a context effect as a personality setting. Raising the tier changes capability when the problem is contaminated context — the same model reviews well once it is independent. Fixing the temperature removes variance and leaves the reviewer just as anchored to its own reasoning.

question: Your CI reviewer emits roughly 400 findings a week, and the two engineers who triage them can read about 80. You want those 80 to be the ones most likely to be real defects. Which approach routes the review attention soundly?
options: Route by the model's raw confidence scores as they are reported
Review a fixed random 5% so the sample stays unbiased overall
Calibrate reported confidence on labelled data, then route by it
Review the largest diffs first, since size tracks review difficulty
explanation: Confidence becomes a usable routing signal only once it has been calibrated against a labelled set. After that, review capacity can be pointed at the genuinely uncertain cases.
wrongAnswerNotes: Raw self-reported confidence is the right signal in its known-unreliable form, which is the closest wrong answer here. A fixed random sample measures the error rate well and routes nobody towards where errors concentrate. Diff size is a weak proxy: a one-line authorisation change outranks a large formatting sweep.

question: A single analyze_document tool handles extraction, summarisation and claim verification, selected by a mode parameter, and the agent keeps choosing the wrong mode. What is the recommended redesign?
options: Document each mode's selection criteria fully in the description
Add a mode that inspects the request and picks a mode itself
Split it into purpose-specific tools with their own contracts
Drop to two modes by folding extraction into summarisation
explanation: Splitting turns a hidden mode decision into a visible tool selection, which is what descriptions are good at guiding. Each tool then has one job and one input and output contract.
wrongAnswerNotes: Documenting the modes better improves the manual for a structure that stays ambiguous — the closest wrong answer, and the one that leaves the decision buried in a parameter. An auto-detect mode buries the same decision one layer deeper. Merging two of the three reduces the options while keeping the overloaded design.

question: When your extraction MCP tool cannot parse a document, it returns "Error: could not parse document" as an ordinary text result, and the agent treats that sentence as document content. What is the correct pattern?
options: Return the failure with the MCP isError flag set on the result
Return a JSON body with an error field the agent reads in the text
Raise an unhandled exception and let the connection drop
Prefix the message with SYSTEM ERROR so the agent notices it
explanation: The protocol has a channel for this. Setting the error flag makes the failure a machine-recognisable condition rather than text that happens to describe one.
wrongAnswerNotes: A structured JSON body improves the error's shape and still arrives as a successful result, so the agent has to infer failure from the payload — the closest wrong answer. A prefix relies on the same inference with less structure. Dropping the connection turns a recoverable tool error into a transport failure.

question: A scanned TIFF arrives in a pipeline that supports PDF and DOCX only, and the extraction tool refuses it. The agent has now retried the same document four times in a row and burned most of the run's tool budget. Which error response would let it respond correctly instead?
options: A business category, retryable false, and a readable reason
A validation category marked retryable, so the agent adjusts its parameters and retries the same document
The parser's full internal diagnostic output, so nothing is lost
A success result with an empty extraction object attached to it
explanation: The key facts the agent needs are isRetryable: false plus a readable reason — no retry or parameter change can make a TIFF into a supported format, so marking it retryable guarantees more wasted attempts. The pipeline's supported-format rule makes 'business' a reasonable category (validation is defensible too); what stops the retry loop is the non-retryable flag and an explanation the agent can act on.
wrongAnswerNotes: Labelling it a validation error invites the agent to reformulate a request that will be refused identically every time — the sharpest trap, since both categories describe refusals. An empty success turns a refusal into silent misinformation. Internal diagnostics are detail the agent cannot act on and should not relay.

question: Extraction runs at 96% field accuracy on clean digital invoices from your three largest vendors, and falls to about 70% on smaller suppliers whose invoices use multi-column layouts, stamped totals, and line items split across pages. Which technique most improves handling of the varied formats?
options: Normalise every document into one layout before extraction runs
Describe every layout the pipeline may encounter in the prompt
Add more worked examples of the clean layout already handled well
Add worked examples covering several genuinely different layouts
explanation: Examples spanning genuinely different structures let the model generalise its judgement to layouts nobody anticipated, which is the documented strength of few-shot prompting for extraction.
wrongAnswerNotes: More examples of the format that already works reinforce the case that is not failing. Enumerating layouts in prose underspecifies each one and grows without end. Pre-normalising every document is brittle and discards the structure the extraction depends on.

question: Your pipeline asks Claude to "respond with JSON" in plain text, and downstream parsing breaks on markdown fences, trailing commentary and the occasional syntax error. What is the reliable structural fix?
options: Switch the format to YAML, whose syntax is more forgiving
Define the extraction as a tool and read the tool_use input
Strengthen the prompt to demand valid JSON and nothing else
Post-process with regexes that strip fences and repair syntax
explanation: With tool use the extraction arrives as schema-conformant tool input rather than prose that happens to contain JSON, so syntax errors are eliminated by construction rather than caught afterwards.
wrongAnswerNotes: A firmer instruction improves the odds inside a channel that is still fundamentally free text. Regex repair patches symptoms and breaks on the first unanticipated shape. Moving to a more forgiving syntax relocates the same unconstrained-text problem.

question: Your extractor has three tools — extract_invoice, extract_receipt and extract_po — each with its own schema. At call time you do not know the document's type, but the pipeline requires a structured extraction on every document and must never receive a free-text reply. Which tool_choice configuration meets this?
options: Left at the default, validating the reply and retrying whenever it is not structured
Forced to extract_invoice by default, re-classifying afterwards if fields do not fit
any, so the model must call a tool and picks the schema that fits the document
auto, together with a system-prompt instruction to always call one of the tools
explanation: Requiring a call while leaving the choice open is exactly the stated requirement: structured output is guaranteed, and the model still selects the schema matching the document in front of it.
wrongAnswerNotes: The automatic setting permits a text reply, so an instruction to always call something stays probabilistic. Forcing one named tool guarantees structure and welds every document to the invoice schema when three types arrive. Leaving the default and retrying is that same permissive setting with cleanup bolted on. Every option here is a real tool_choice state; the item is about telling them apart.

question: Your extraction schema marks several fields as required, but many source documents legitimately omit them — a purchase order with no tax line, for instance. On those documents the model invents plausible values to satisfy the required fields. You need absent data represented honestly without breaking the schema contract. What is the right change?
options: Add an enum sentinel such as NOT_PRESENT as an allowed value on each field
Keep them required, attach per-field confidence, and drop low values later
Split extraction into always-present and sometimes-present tools
Make those fields optional and nullable so the model can return null instead
explanation: A required field on information that may not exist leaves the model no honest answer. Nullable fields give it a legitimate way to report that the source is silent, and the extraction still validates.
wrongAnswerNotes: A sentinel value bolts a null substitute onto every field type and pushes the special case into every downstream consumer. Splitting by presence is brittle, because which fields are absent varies document by document rather than type by type. A confidence filter still starts from a fabricated value and only hopes to catch it afterwards.

question: An invoice extraction comes back failing schema validation with two specific field errors: a date in the wrong format, and a total typed as a string rather than a number. You intend to retry. What should the retry request contain, and when should you stop retrying altogether?
options: Document, failed output and errors; stop when the source lacks it
A fresh prompt with no reference to the failure; stop on API errors
The errors and a stricter instruction; stop after two failures
The failed output and the errors only, to keep the retry cheap
explanation: Self-correction needs all three inputs: what the model produced, what was wrong with it, and the source to re-ground against. The boundary matters too — formatting and structural errors are recoverable, information absent from the document is not.
wrongAnswerNotes: Dropping the source document leaves the model correcting fields it can no longer see, which is why cheap retries plateau and is the closest wrong answer here. A fresh prompt withholds the feedback that makes a retry targeted. Stopping on API errors inverts the rule, since those are precisely the transient kind worth retrying.

question: An overnight batch of 10,000 documents finishes with 200 failures — mostly oversized documents that exceeded the context limit, plus a few transient errors. What is the correct recovery?
options: Send the 200 to the synchronous API unchanged, where they fit
Log the 200 for weekly review and treat the batch as complete
Resubmit failures by custom_id, chunking oversized documents
Resubmit all 10,000 and keep whichever results arrive first
explanation: The custom identifier correlates each response back to its request, so the failures can be isolated, fixed at the cause by chunking, and resubmitted alone — paying again for 200 documents rather than 10,000.
wrongAnswerNotes: Resubmitting everything reprocesses 9,800 successes to recover 200. Sending oversized documents down a different API path unchanged misreads where the limit lives: it belongs to the model, so they fail synchronously too. Logging for later quietly drops two percent of the corpus.

question: An extraction pipeline reports 97% accuracy on a 5,000-document labelled holdout, and a manager proposes cutting human review to a 2% random sample. The corpus mixes clean digital invoices, scanned faxes and handwritten receipts, and fields range from printed USD totals to handwritten dates. Select TWO practices that must come first.
options: Break accuracy down by document type and field, since the aggregate hides segments
Sample high-confidence extractions on a stratified basis to keep measuring
Accept the aggregate, since 97% already exceeds the reviewers' own accuracy
Route to human review only those extractions where a required field came back null
Raise the model's confidence threshold uniformly across every field until error clears
explanation: Two safeguards make the cut defensible: segmentation shows whether handwritten dates on scanned faxes sit far below the 97% headline, and stratified sampling keeps measuring the population the humans have stopped checking.
wrongAnswerNotes: Null-only routing catches missing values and misses the confidently wrong ones that are present and incorrect. A uniform threshold ignores that calibration differs sharply by field and by document type. Accepting the aggregate because it beats human reviewers on average says nothing about the segments where it does not.

question: Your customer support agent uses a while loop that checks whether the assistant's response contains "Is there anything else I can help with?" to determine when to stop the agentic loop. In testing, the loop sometimes terminates prematurely. What should you change?
options: Inspect whether the response includes any tool_use content blocks and use their presence as the sole continuation signal
Add a broader set of closing phrases and fallback regex patterns to the text-based termination check
Set a maximum iteration count as the primary loop control, falling back to text parsing only when the cap is reached
Check the stop_reason field in the API response: continue the agentic loop when it returns "tool_use" and terminate when it returns "end_turn"
explanation: The stop_reason field is the definitive API signal for loop control. Parsing natural language for termination cues is fragile. Iteration caps are safety nets, not primary stopping mechanisms. Principle: Use stop_reason as the sole loop control signal. Never parse natural language to determine loop termination.

question: Your agent handles billing disputes. When a customer mentions an order number, the agent calls get_customer with it (wrong input type), gets an error, then calls lookup_order with the customer's name, retrieves the wrong account, and issues a refund to the wrong person. Which change most effectively prevents this?
options: Block downstream tools until get_customer returns a verified ID, and expand tool descriptions to specify accepted input types
Implement a routing classifier that analyzes each incoming request, determines the correct tool sequence, and pre-selects tools before the agent runs
Add few-shot examples showing the correct verification-then-lookup sequence and reinforce the ordering with explicit system prompt instructions
Consolidate get_customer and lookup_order into a single unified tool that internally determines the appropriate backend query based on identifier format
explanation: This is a compound problem: skipped verification AND wrong tool inputs. Programmatic prerequisites guarantee ordering; improved descriptions prevent input confusion. Principle: When errors have financial consequences, combine programmatic enforcement for ordering with clear tool descriptions for correct usage.

question: Your agent receives: "I need to return my damaged laptop from order #1234, I was overcharged $15 on order #5678, and I want to cancel my subscription." Logs show the agent addresses the return, then summarizes the other two as "billing concerns" in a handoff. What should you change?
options: Add a post-processing validator that checks whether every order number mentioned in the original message appears in the final resolution
Decompose multi-concern requests into distinct items, investigate each, then synthesize a unified resolution
Limit customer messages to one issue at a time using an input pre-processing filter that detects compound requests
Increase the agent's max_tokens to allow responses long enough to address all issues in a single turn
explanation: The agent fails to decompose and track multiple concerns. Explicit decomposition with parallel investigation and unified synthesis is the fix. Principle: Multi-concern requests require explicit decomposition, independent investigation, and unified synthesis.

question: Your agent's escalation prompt says: "Escalate when you are not confident." Logs show the agent confidently processes competitor price matching — a scenario not in company policy — and invents a 10% discount. What's the most effective fix?
options: Add explicit escalation criteria such as "escalate when policy is ambiguous or silent on the request" with few-shot examples of policy gap scenarios
Implement a confidence threshold that triggers human escalation when self-reported score falls below 7/10
Deploy sentiment analysis to detect unusual or unexpected customer requests and flag them for human review before the agent responds
Create a comprehensive policy knowledge base covering every possible customer request scenario and update it weekly with new edge cases
explanation: The agent was confident because it could generate a plausible response — LLM confidence doesn't correlate with policy coverage. Principle: Escalation criteria must include policy gaps and ambiguity. LLMs can be confidently wrong when policy is silent.

question: A customer writes: "I want to talk to a real person, not a bot." The agent responds: "Let me first look into your account — what's your order number?" The customer replies: "No, I want a human NOW." What should have happened?
options: The agent should escalate now after the second explicit request, since offering to help first was a reasonable customer service attempt
Escalate to a human agent immediately on the first explicit request, without attempting investigation or account lookup first
Continue investigating since most customers are satisfied once their issue is resolved
Ask the customer to briefly describe their issue before routing, so the human agent receives adequate context for a warm handoff
explanation: When a customer explicitly requests a human agent, immediate escalation is required without attempting investigation. Principle: Explicit customer requests for human agents must be honored immediately.

question: Your PostToolUse hook normalizes dates from get_customer (Unix timestamps) and lookup_order (ISO 8601). Without it, the agent sometimes miscompares dates. A colleague suggests moving normalization to the system prompt instead. What's the correct assessment?
options: Modify the MCP tools themselves to return a single consistent date format, eliminating the need for either hook-based or prompt-based normalization
The hook is correct: deterministic normalization before model processing eliminates compounding format conversion failures across interactions
Both approaches are functionally equivalent for this use case since Claude reliably handles both timestamp formats in its training data
The prompt approach is simpler and Claude handles date format conversion reliably
explanation: Hooks provide deterministic data transformation before the model sees the data. Prompt-based conversion works most of the time but has compounding failure rates. Principle: Use hooks for deterministic guarantees; use prompts where probabilistic compliance is acceptable.

question: Your refund hook blocks process_refund calls over $500, redirecting to human escalation. A PM asks to replace it with a prompt instruction, arguing hooks are "too rigid" for borderline cases like $501. How should you respond?
options: Implement both: keep the hook as a hard backstop alongside prompt instructions for nuanced handling
Replace the hook with a detailed prompt that includes few-shot examples demonstrating proper reasoning about borderline refund amounts near the $500 threshold
Replace with a graduated range: auto-approve under $400, escalate over $600, let the agent use judgment for the $400–$600 gray zone based on case context
Keep the hook for enforcement — if the $500 threshold needs nuance, adjust the business rule itself rather than making compliance probabilistic
explanation: The PM's concern is valid, but refine the business rule, not the enforcement mechanism. Financial compliance needs deterministic enforcement. Principle: When business rules require guaranteed compliance, programmatic enforcement is non-negotiable.

question: When escalating, your system passes the full conversation transcript. Human agents spend 5–7 minutes reading before helping. Handle time increased 40%. What should you implement?
options: Reduce the maximum conversation length before mandatory escalation occurs, keeping transcripts short enough for human agents to scan quickly
Train agents to skim transcripts faster using a keyword highlighting tool that surfaces key sentences
Pass only the last 3 exchanges to reduce reading time, supplemented by a one-line summary of the customer's original request for earlier context
Compile a structured handoff summary including customer ID, verified issues, root cause analysis, actions already taken, and recommended next steps
explanation: A structured handoff summary gives human agents everything needed without reading full transcripts. Principle: Structured handoff summaries enable efficient human takeover without transcript review.

question: get_customer returns 42 fields per record but only 5 are needed. After 4–5 tool calls, the agent gives inconsistent answers referencing wrong customer data. What's the most effective fix?
options: Set a maximum turn count and force new sessions to prevent verbose tool output from accumulating beyond a manageable threshold
Add the customer ID prefix to every agent response so both the agent and customer can detect cross-account confusion early
Implement a PostToolUse hook that trims each tool response to only the fields relevant to the current task before they enter context
Upgrade to a model with a larger context window to accommodate the additional field data
explanation: 42 fields × 4-5 calls creates noise that degrades model attention. Trimming to needed fields reduces context pollution. Principle: Trim verbose tool outputs to relevant fields before they accumulate in context.

question: lookup_order returns an empty array for a mistyped order number. The agent tells the customer "I don't see any orders on your account." The customer actually mistyped. What should change about the tool's response?
options: Automatically search for similar order numbers using fuzzy matching and return the closest match along with a confidence score for the agent to evaluate
Implement retry logic that tries common input variations such as adding or removing leading zeros, dashes, and whitespace before returning empty
Return structured metadata distinguishing this as a successful query with no matches, and include a suggestion for the agent to verify the identifier with the customer
Return isError: true whenever no results are found so the agent recognizes something unexpected occurred and can attempt recovery or clarification
explanation: Empty results and access failures must be distinguishable. The agent needs metadata to know the query succeeded but found nothing. Principle: Distinguish access failures from valid empty results in tool responses.

question: You're A/B testing escalation prompts. Version A: "Only escalate when you cannot resolve after exhausting all tools." Version B lists 4 specific criteria: customer requests human, policy gap, no progress after 2 tool calls, policy exception. Which performs better?
options: Version B — explicit categorical criteria provide clear decision boundaries that produce consistent escalation behavior across diverse case types
Version A — simpler instructions give the agent more autonomy to develop judgment across scenarios
Version B initially for new deployments, but Version A performs better once the agent has processed enough historical cases to learn escalation patterns organically
Both perform equivalently since the underlying model capabilities are identical regardless of how the escalation prompt is worded or structured
explanation: Explicit criteria outperform vague guidance because they define clear boundaries. LLMs don't learn across sessions. Principle: Explicit categorical criteria consistently outperform vague directional guidance.

question: get_customer returns three matches for an email. The agent selects the most recently active account and processes a refund. What should it have done?
options: Escalate to a human agent since multiple matches on a single email address indicate a data quality issue requiring backend investigation
Select the personal account rather than business accounts since the customer used a personal communication channel to make contact
Process the refund for all three accounts to ensure the correct customer is covered regardless of which account is theirs
Ask the customer for additional identifying information such as full name, phone number, or account number to disambiguate between the matches
explanation: Multiple matches require clarification, not heuristic selection. Principle: When tool results return multiple matches, request additional identifiers rather than selecting based on heuristics.

question: Progressive summarization causes the agent to say "some issues with your recent order" instead of referencing the specific $47.99 overcharge on order #4521 from March 15. What went wrong?
options: The summarization interval triggers too aggressively — increase the number of turns before summarization fires to preserve more raw conversation history
Disable summarization entirely and accept the higher token costs as a necessary tradeoff to preserve full conversation fidelity across long sessions
Extract transactional facts (amounts, dates, order numbers) into a persistent block outside summarized history
Switch to a model with a larger context window so summarization isn't triggered and the full conversation history remains available for reference
explanation: Numerical values and identifiers are lost in summarization. A persistent "case facts" block preserves critical details. Principle: Extract transactional facts into a persistent structured block outside summarized history.

question: Your agent handles a straightforward damage replacement (photo provided, within return window, eligible) but escalates instead of processing. The system prompt says: "When in doubt, always escalate to protect the customer." What should you change?
options: Add a confidence scoring mechanism that calculates a numerical score before each action and only triggers escalation when confidence drops below 50%
Replace with specific criteria defining when to escalate (policy gaps, customer requests) and when to resolve autonomously
Qualify the instruction: "when in doubt, escalate — unless the case matches a documented workflow with verifiable eligibility"
Remove all escalation instructions entirely and let the agent handle every case autonomously based on its own assessment of whether it can resolve the issue
explanation: "When in doubt, always escalate" creates over-escalation bias. Specific criteria define clear boundaries. Principle: Vague safety instructions create over-escalation bias. Define both escalation AND resolution conditions.
